rows.title: Ottawa amends, extends tariff relief program beyond U.S. steel imports
rows.summary: Ottawa is extending by one year, to June 30, 2028, its temporary remission program, which gives relief to Canadian companies that import U.S. goods hit by Canada's own retaliatory tariffs. The program now also covers non-steel goods used in mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction, plus goods bought by public education bodies, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations. Goods that Canadian suppliers can reliably provide will lose relief: certain trailers on Dec. 1, and aluminum wire, aluminum extrusions and paperboard products on Feb. 1, 2027, to push buyers toward domestic suppliers. Canada widened its retaliation in September when a new round of U.S. duties took effect, and now charges counter-tariffs of 15 to 50 per cent on a range of U.S. goods. The government therefore has to balance protecting Canadian producers against raising costs for Canadian firms that rely on U.S. inputs.
rows.fact: On Nov. 9 the federal government extended its relief program for firms importing tariffed U.S. goods to June 30, 2028, and widened which goods qualify. Some goods that can be made in Canada will lose relief starting Dec. 1, 2026 and Feb. 1, 2027. Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said the changes balance supporting companies now with encouraging them to buy Canadian-made goods.
rows.outlook: The article notes the Canadian Steel Producers Association has argued in the past that the program weakens firms' incentive to switch to Canadian suppliers.
rows.why: 보복관세가 외국뿐 아니라 자국 기업의 비용도 올린다는 점과, 정부가 '관세 면제(remission)'로 그 부담을 조절하는 방식을 실제 사례로 이해할 수 있다.
rows.why_en: It is a real example of how retaliatory tariffs also raise costs for a country's own businesses, and how a government uses tariff exemptions to manage that trade-off.
rows.term_def: A government decision to waive or refund a tariff that would normally be charged on certain imports, often used when domestic companies have no practical alternative to the foreign product.
rows.note: Checked against the Department of Finance Canada news release of Nov. 9, 2026, which confirms the 2028 extension, expanded coverage, removal dates and the 15-50% counter-tariffs.

opinion.title: Remission orders blunt Ottawa's new countertariffs on 629 U.S. goods, trade analysts say
opinion.author: The Hub Staff (citing economist Trevor Tombe)
opinion.summary: This analysis argues that Ottawa's Sept. 8 counter-tariffs on 629 U.S. tariff lines, covering about $27.6 billion of imports, are matched dollar-for-dollar mainly on paper, because remission relief already covers roughly one in three targeted lines and more than 60% of steel and aluminum lines. Citing economist Trevor Tombe, it notes that about four in five dollars of Canada-U.S. trade are intermediate inputs, which limits how hard Canada can retaliate without hurting its own manufacturers. It concludes that narrow, steel-focused protection makes more sense than broad retaliation. It predates the Nov. 9 changes but covers the same remission program.
opinion.why: 관세 정책의 '발표된 세율'과 '실제로 걷히는 세금'이 어떻게 다를 수 있는지, 그리고 보복관세에 왜 한계가 있는지 비판적으로 생각해 볼 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: It helps students think critically about how a tariff's announced rate can differ from what is actually collected, and why retaliation has limits.

rows.title: Fed's Waller plans to support at least a quarter-point rate hike in December
rows.summary: Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said on Nov. 10 at a conference in London that he will back at least a 0.25 percentage-point increase in the Fed's policy rate at its Dec. 8-9 meeting, even if October inflation turns out softer than September's. He added that the Fed should consider a bigger half-point hike if core consumer prices rose 0.3% or more in October, since a smaller move could hurt the Fed's credibility as an inflation fighter. He pointed to September PCE inflation of 3.7%, far above the 2% target, and said energy costs and AI-related hardware prices could keep inflation high into 2027. He called the labor market solid, with unemployment at 4.1%, and expects growth to slow from 3.4% last quarter while staying healthy. Treasury yields rose after his remarks, a sign that borrowing for homes, cars and businesses could get more expensive.
rows.fact: Speaking before the October CPI release, Waller said he supports a December rate hike in any case, and possibly a half-point hike if core inflation is hot. Futures markets put roughly an 85% chance on a December hike, while Reuters noted that Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has avoided giving guidance on the rate path.
rows.outlook: Futures pricing implies the Fed's target range would rise to 4.00%-4.25% after a December hike, with another hike possible by March.
rows.why: 물가를 잡기 위해 중앙은행이 금리를 올리는 이유와, 그 결정이 대출 금리와 채권 시장에 어떻게 퍼지는지 실제 사례로 배울 수 있다.
rows.why_en: It shows, with a live example, why a central bank raises interest rates to fight inflation and how that decision spreads to loan rates and bond markets.
rows.term_def: The rise in prices leaving out food and energy, whose prices swing a lot. Central banks watch it to see the underlying trend of inflation.
rows.note: Remarks by a Fed governor on Nov. 10 (policy signal, not a formal decision). October CPI was due the same morning in the U.S. and is not reflected here.

opinion.title: Fed rate hike may not be 'one and done' if AI boom fuels inflation
opinion.author: Mary Helen Gillespie (Fed and economy reporter)
opinion.summary: This news analysis, which ends with the author's own view, asks whether the Fed's expected December hike will be its last. It cites Richmond Fed President Thomas Barkin, who says AI infrastructure spending is pushing up near-term inflation, and Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee, who warns about overheating and inflation spreading across sectors. It notes the October jobs report beat expectations and that UBS and the Mortgage Bankers Association's chief economist expect more hikes into early 2027. The author argues a single hike looks less and less likely if overheating persists.
opinion.why: 인공지능 투자 붐 같은 산업 변화가 물가와 금리에까지 영향을 준다는 점을 보여 주어, 경제의 여러 부분이 서로 연결되어 있음을 이해하는 데 도움이 된다.
opinion.why_en: It shows how a new trend like the AI investment boom can affect prices and interest rates, helping students see how different parts of the economy are linked.

rows.title: Korea's export boom masks widening gap between large, small firms
rows.original_source: The Korea Times (data: Ministry of Data and Statistics, Korea Customs Service)
rows.summary: Preliminary official data released Nov. 10 by the Ministry of Data and Statistics and the Korea Customs Service show South Korea's third-quarter exports jumped 72.3% from a year earlier to $318.6 billion, while imports rose 25% to $203.1 billion. The gains were heavily concentrated: large corporations' exports more than doubled (up 103.5%) to $248.6 billion, while medium-sized firms grew 12.8% and small firms only 10.7%. The top 10 exporters' share of all shipments rose to 60.9% from 40.5% a year earlier, driven by electrical and electronics exports, including semiconductors, which rose 143.6% to $206 billion. The number of exporting companies barely grew (0.3%, to 69,988), suggesting the chip-led boom is not spreading widely across the economy.
rows.fact: Q3 exports rose 72.3% year-on-year to $318.6 billion, accelerating from 38.4% growth in Q1 and 57.2% in Q2. Large firms' export growth was nearly ten times that of small firms, and the top 100 exporters now account for 79.4% of exports.
rows.outlook: The Korea Institute of Finance projects growth to slow to 3.1% in 2027 from an estimated 3.8% in 2026 and warns that heavy chip dependence leaves the economy exposed to any pullback in AI investment.
rows.why: 수출 기록 뒤에 숨은 대기업·중소기업 격차를 통해 경제 성장의 '속도'와 '분배'가 어떻게 다를 수 있는지 이해할 수 있다.
rows.why_en: It shows how record headline export numbers can hide a widening gap between big and small firms, helping you see the difference between how fast an economy grows and how evenly that growth is shared.
rows.term_def: How much of a country's total exports come from a small number of companies or products. High concentration means the economy depends heavily on a few players, such as chipmakers.
rows.note: Official statistics released Nov. 10; figures confirmed by Yonhap's report on the same release.

opinion.title: AI is hiding the cracks in South Korea's economy
opinion.author: Daniel Moss (Bloomberg Opinion columnist)
opinion.summary: Moss argues that the AI-driven chip boom is producing spectacular headline numbers for Korea, with chip shipments surging, annual exports on track to pass $1 trillion and repeated GDP upgrades. Beneath that, he points to weak household consumption, heavy household debt, an uneven job market and rising youth unemployment. He adds long-term risks, including one of the world's lowest fertility rates and Chinese competitors eroding Korea's strengths in batteries, ships and petrochemicals. If the AI boom fades, he warns, Korea would fall back on industries where its edge is shrinking.
opinion.why: 반도체 호황이 경제 전체의 건강을 보장하지 않는다는 시각을 통해 한 산업에 의존하는 경제의 위험을 생각해 볼 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: It challenges the idea that a chip boom means the whole economy is healthy, and gets you thinking about the risks of depending on one industry.

rows.title: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%, the first increase for more than three years
rows.summary: On Nov. 5 the Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75% to 4%, its first increase in more than three years. Oil has stayed above $100 a barrel for months because of the Iran conflict and the stalled reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, pushing UK CPI inflation up to 3.5% in September. The Bank now expects inflation to peak at about 4.9% in mid-2027, far above its July forecast of 3.2%, partly because the Ofgem household energy price cap is expected to rise sharply in January. The hike makes mortgages more expensive, and the Monetary Policy Committee expects households' real post-tax incomes to fall this year and next.
rows.fact: Eight of the nine MPC members voted for the quarter-point rise, and Catherine Mann wanted a half-point increase. Governor Andrew Bailey said the move should not be read as the start of a long run of hikes, but that it is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict is resolved. The Bank expects the budget's fuel duty freeze and VAT cut on electricity to lower inflation by about a quarter point in mid-2027.
rows.outlook: Oxford Economics' Andrew Goodwin said another hike in December or February is likely; the next decision is due Dec. 17.
rows.why: 중동 전쟁으로 인한 에너지 가격 충격이 물가를 끌어올리고, 중앙은행의 금리 인상이 가계의 대출 이자와 실질 소득에 어떤 영향을 미치는지 한눈에 보여 준다.
rows.why_en: It shows step by step how an energy price shock from a war abroad pushes up inflation, and how a central bank's rate rise in response changes families' mortgage costs and real incomes.
rows.term_def: The interest rate the Bank of England pays on money commercial banks keep with it. Raising it makes borrowing more expensive across the economy, which cools spending and helps bring inflation down.
rows.note: 7-day fallback (decision on Nov. 5 UK time). Key figures cross-checked against MoneyWeek's live coverage of the decision.

opinion.title: Hawkish Bank of England hikes rates, and there's more to come
opinion.author: James Smith (Developed Markets Economist, UK, ING)
opinion.summary: Smith calls the hike more hawkish than expected because every MPC member backed a rise, the Bank's 4.9% inflation peak is above most forecasts, and some officials signalled more tightening. He argues the consensus for a further hike is weaker than it looks, since some members see this as a one-off insurance move and services inflation is expected to stay broadly flat. He also judges the risk of energy costs spreading into wider prices to be much lower than in 2022, given a cooling jobs market and tight fiscal policy. ING's base case is one more quarter-point hike by February 2027, followed by cuts from around late 2027.
opinion.why: 같은 금리 인상 결정을 두고도 전문가들이 향후 물가와 금리 경로를 다르게 해석한다는 점을 보여 주어, 경제 전망이 데이터와 가정에 따라 달라짐을 배울 수 있다.
opinion.why_en: It shows how experts can read the same rate decision differently when forecasting inflation and interest rates, teaching that economic outlooks depend on data and assumptions.

rows.title: Bank of Japan debated need for faster rate hikes, October summary shows
rows.summary: On Nov. 10 the Bank of Japan published its Summary of Opinions from its Oct. 29-30 policy meeting, showing some board members wanted to raise interest rates faster because underlying inflation has reached the bank's 2% target. At that meeting the BOJ kept its key rate at 1.25%, said it had finally met its price goal, and flagged upside risks to prices as a weak yen raises energy and import costs. Other members urged caution, pointing to soft consumption, doubts about how long AI-related demand will last, and the delay before past hikes take full effect. The board's views matter for borrowing costs, the yen and Japan's recovery from decades of deflation.
rows.fact: One member said the next hike should come without the BOJ becoming overly cautious, and two members wanted the policy rate moved to a neutral level soon. Staff estimate the neutral rate at 1.1% to 2.5%, and the BOJ already raised rates in June and September this year.
rows.outlook: Most analysts in a Reuters poll expect a hike to 1.5% in December, with a peak rate of 1.75% or 2%.
rows.why: 중앙은행이 물가 목표를 달성한 뒤 금리를 얼마나 빨리 올릴지를 두고 내부 의견이 어떻게 갈리는지 보여 주어, 금리·환율·경기의 연결 고리를 이해하는 데 좋은 사례다.
rows.why_en: It shows how a central bank's board splits over how fast to raise rates once its inflation goal is met, a clear case study of how interest rates, currencies and growth are linked.
rows.term_def: The interest rate that neither speeds up nor slows down the economy. Above it, policy cools growth and inflation; below it, policy stimulates them.
rows.note: BOJ released the Summary of Opinions on the morning of Nov. 10 JST; body also read on The Standard (HK) republication.

opinion.title: Why Japan's Monetary Policy is Failing to Lift the Yen
opinion.author: Scott Danaher (contributing author)
opinion.summary: The piece starts from the BOJ's Nov. 10 Summary of Opinions, which signalled a possible December hike, and notes the yen still traded above 158 per dollar. It reviews Japan's currency interventions earlier this year and how quickly their effect faded. The author argues the main driver of yen weakness is the wide gap between the BOJ's 1.25% rate and the Fed's 3.75-4.00%, which makes the carry trade attractive, with public debt of about 200% of GDP adding pressure. Intervention, he concludes, is only a temporary brake unless the rate gap narrows meaningfully.
opinion.why: 금리 인상 신호에도 엔화가 약세인 이유를 금리 차이와 재정 문제로 설명해, 통화정책이 환율에 미치는 효과의 한계를 생각해 보게 한다.
opinion.why_en: It explains why the yen stays weak despite signals of higher rates, pointing to the rate gap and fiscal problems, and makes readers think about the limits of monetary policy's effect on exchange rates.
